description: FireLedger turns two decades of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent record and a tool people can act on.
summary: FireLedger turns two decades of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent record and a tool people can act on. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) see fire very differently: VIIRS pixels are smaller and catch cooler fires, so raw counts jump when sensors change and can't be compared over time. We harmonized both into a single unit, "VIIRS-equivalent fire-cell-days", by gridding detections to 1 km cells and calibrating MODIS to VIIRS over their 2012–2026 overlap. On top of that record, FireLedger shows a year-by-month burning activity calendar for any area a user draws, picks or types, compares the current month with the historical median, and exports CSV, charts and a PDF briefing. When live hotspots appear, it produces a transparent Response & Logistics Advisory. It matters because fire managers, farmers and communities need to know whether this season is normal, using data that stays consistent as satellites retire, including Suomi NPP on 2 Nov 2026.
details:
FireLedger (https://fireledger.earth) is a web application that turns more than two decades of NASA FIRMS active-fire detections into one consistent, sensor-independent record of burning activity. The MODIS instruments have observed fire since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012, but they see fire very differently: VIIRS pixels are about seven times smaller and detect cooler, smaller fires, so raw hotspot counts jump whenever the satellite mix changes. Our goal was to remove that artefact so users see real patterns, trends and anomalies rather than satellite quirks.

To do this, we built a reproducible Python pipeline that downloads FIRMS country archives and area-API data for MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS on Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. It uses standard-processing data wherever available and near-real-time data only for the most recent days, never both for the same date. It keeps vegetation fires with nominal or high confidence and snaps every detection to a 0.01-degree grid. Counting unique fire cells per day, rather than raw pixels, removes most of the resolution difference between sensors. A seasonal calibration model, selected by leave-one-year-out cross-validation over the 2012–2026 overlap, then converts the 2000–2011 MODIS record into "VIIRS-equivalent fire-cell-days". For Morocco, our demo region from December 2000 to November 2026, harmonization reduced the monthly error from 76 to 24 fire-cell-days (R² 0.66, bias +0.6%). The calendar's busiest month, July 2022, matches the major fires reported in Larache, Ouezzane, Taza and Tetouan. Anomalies are measured against the historical median with robust z-scores and percentiles, and long-term trends use the Theil-Sen slope with a Mann-Kendall significance test.

In the app, a user chooses an area by drawing a rectangle or polygon, searching a place, picking a region or entering coordinates and a radius, then sets a date range. FireLedger answers with a year-by-month burning activity calendar, colored by counts or by anomaly. A "This month vs history" panel gives the current value, the median, its percentile and rank, and a plain-language "Is this normal?" sentence. Annual totals with a trend line, a seasonal profile, the ten busiest months, a radial Fire Season Clock and a time-lapse map complete the picture. Users can compare two areas side by side, save watch zones, and download the hotspot data, the calendar and anomaly table, every chart, and a one-page PDF Fire Situation Briefing.

When satellites detect hotspots in the selected area during the last 48 hours, FireLedger opens a Response & Logistics Advisory. This rule-based engine combines fire intensity, clustering and persistence with the historical anomaly, live wind and humidity from Open-Meteo, and nearby settlements, hospitals, water points and possible staging sites from OpenStreetMap. It assigns a severity tier from Monitor to Emergency and suggests the resources to mobilize. It also shows the likely downwind direction and gives population-protection and smoke-health advice along with local emergency numbers. Every recommendation shows why it was triggered, and the advisory can be shared as a short SMS or WhatsApp message or downloaded as a PDF. It is clearly presented as decision support, not an official order, and reminds users to follow their local civil protection authorities.

The intended impact is to give fire services, foresters, researchers, farmers and communities a reliable answer to the question "is this fire season unusual here?", and a fast first briefing when fire is detected. Because the record is anchored to VIIRS, it continues seamlessly on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 now that Suomi NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026.

We developed the pipeline in Python with pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, Matplotlib and pytest, and the web application in TypeScript with Vite, MapLibre GL, D3 and jsPDF. The app runs on AWS: Amplify Hosting serves the site and redeploys automatically from GitHub, Lambda functions in Python 3.12 provide the API, S3 caches FIRMS responses, EventBridge refreshes live data every three hours, and SSM Parameter Store keeps the FIRMS key server-side so it is never exposed to the browser. An AI coding assistant (Claude Code) helped write and test code and documentation. The team defined the method, data choices and design, and all validation figures come from the pipeline run on FIRMS data.

Throughout the project we weighed accessibility, transparency and real-world use. The color ramps are colorblind-safe blue-to-orange scales, every chart has a "Read as table" view, the whole interface works with the keyboard, and it scores 100 for accessibility in Lighthouse. The app installs as a lightweight PWA with an offline cache for low-bandwidth field use, and it speaks English, French and Arabic with a full right-to-left layout. We were also open about the limits of satellite fire data, such as detection latency, clouds and smoke, non-fire heat sources and the uncertainty of the MODIS backcast, and the app states them wherever they matter. FireLedger was built by Khalid Ammar, Walid Rezagaoui and Imad Labrini.
